articles.title: Bomb threats target seven flights across Europe
articles.summary: Planes in Poland, Spain, Bulgaria and Italy have been checked for explosives following separate threats.
body: Watch: Sniffer dog inspects Ryanair plane in Spain after suspected bomb threat
Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.

Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian air force until landing.
Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.

It is unclear if the incidents are connected. While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.
The UK government described today's incidents as "malicious hoax threats".

In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".
Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".

A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.
Two of the four flights were en route to Warsaw Chopin airport
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.
"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."
"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.

Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.
"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.
He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.
The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.

Bulgaria's border police said in a statement sent to the BBC that at around 10:35 local time (08:35 GMT) it had received an email about "the presence of an improvised explosive device on a flight returning from Bergamo".
"Standard procedures for such incidents were immediately activated, and an operational headquarters comprising representatives of various institutions was convened," the statement said.
The border police added that the same email also reported a "similar threat against aircraft arriving from Dublin".
These incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.
BBC Verify has consulted aviation safety experts about what happens on board a plane when a bomb threat is issued.

Marco Chan, a former pilot for Cathay Pacific Airways and Hong Kong Airlines who is now a senior lecturer in aviation operations at Kingston University, said a bomb threat is considered "genuine until it is resolved, even though most turn out to be hoaxes".

Chan said crews will "quietly search" toilets, galleys and storage areas and will not touch a suspicious item unless it has to be taken to an area on the aircraft designated as the least risky bomb location.
The aircraft's captain will have multiple factors to assess, according to former airline pilot Terry Tozer, an aviation safety commentator.
He said these include what facilities are available at the airport they are being diverted to and how the plane can continue onwards should it turn out to be a false threat.
Chan added that once on the ground, the plane is generally "taken to an isolated stand, passengers are disembarked, and police and bomb disposal teams search it".

articles.title: How America voted in maps and charts
articles.summary: See the maps and charts that show how America voted in the US midterm elections.
body: It's been an extraordinary night for the Democrats in the US midterms.
They have taken control of the Senate and the House of Representatives too.

The results in the Senate are beyond what the Democrats would have expected. North Carolina was a likely pick-up but South Carolina was a huge shock and Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932.
Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine have also turned blue and the Democrats held Michigan. There is one toss-up seat to come in Alaska and even Mississippi is now on a knife edge, according to CBS News.
Polls before the election saw South Carolina as leaning Republican. It had been a deep red seat for many years, last returning a Democratic senator in 1998.
The shift from Republican to Democrat happened across the country. For example recent vote share shows Texas moved 9 points towards the Democrats when compared with the 2024 Senate race.
The BBC's partner CBS News projected the Democrats would win the House just after 03:00 GMT on Wednesday (22:00 EST Tuesday).
Now it's a question of how big that win will be as counting continues.
Two significant seats are Florida 14 and Florida 25 which the Democrats have held. This is a blow to the Republicans' attempt to redraw the boundaries in their favour.
The redistricting saw both districts move from having a majority of 2024 Kamala Harris voters to having a majority of people who voted for Donald Trump.
Florida 22, which was also redrawn to favour the Republicans, saw a victory for the Democrats too.
A huge poll of voters suggests women turned out in numbers and most voted Democrat. Men on the other hand were evenly split between the two main parties.

Hispanic voters look to be one of the key groups in the elections in Florida. The poll suggests this group backed the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon by 55% to 44% for the Republican Ashley Moody.
This is a turnaround from the estimated 55% of Hispanic voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024.
The poll also asked what issues voters were most concerned about. It suggests that across the country the economy was the biggest issue, followed by the state of democracy.
When voters were asked if Donald Trump's policies impacted economic conditions, the poll suggests more that two-thirds believe they had made things worse.

articles.title: Key moments from a night of midterm election firsts
articles.summary: Democrats have taken control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency - proving moments of celebration.
body: Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Projected results have provided the party with a number of things to celebrate - and rival Republicans some reasons to commiserate.
These are some of the key moments so far, which include a number of historic firsts.
Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Trump two years ago, registering sizeable swings in the likes of Texas, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina.

Among the senior party figures who have cheered the results are Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the Speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.
Hakeem Jeffries is among the most senior Democrats
"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.

If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next Speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson and becoming the first black person to fill that role.
FOLLOW LIVE: Results and reaction from US midterms
ANALYSIS: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night

Abdul El-Sayed has become the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate - after claiming victory in Michigan in what was one of a handful of closely fought contests. His win means the seat stays in Democratic hands.
He defeated Republican opponent Mike Rogers, who received a surprise last-minute endorsement from El-Sayed's Democratic rival in the primary contest.
The race was one of the bitterest of the midterms. Trump invoked 9/11 and even called El-Sayed a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.
El-Sayed triumphed in one of the bitterest contests of the midterms

El-Sayed's supporters went wild when he took the stage to celebrate his claimed victory, wrote the BBC's Nada Tawfik. He said: "Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say 'inshallah,' or 'God willing,' whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned."
He went on to say: "But today, tonight, we can turn that 'inshallah' into 'alhamdulillah'. For the right-wing ops, that just means 'praise be to God.'"
Trump spoke throughout the evening to a number of US media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".

He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Texas.

Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."
He acknowledged that the US-Israel war on Iran, which has impacted consumer prices in the US, had affected the vote, saying: "Iran was a piece of it."
The defeat of Susan Collins, who has served as the Republican senator for Maine for three decades, was one indicator of the scale of the Republican losses.
She was felled by Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, a logger who sought to point to his background to persuade blue-collar Mainers to vote for him.
In a statement reported by US media, Collins conceded defeat and said it had been the "honour of my life" to serve the state for 30 years.
There was a sombre atmosphere at the watch party for Republican Susan Collins
Collins entered the race as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election, and found that her tactic to distance herself from Trump did not work.
The BBC's Helena Humphrey described a sombre atmosphere at Collins's watch party in the city of Maine - where the song Closing Time was played.

With James Talarico winning a seat in the US Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa being elected state governor, Democrats scored two statewide victories in Texas - ending a string of defeats they have endured for almost two generations.

Talarico's supporters went beserk as the projected results arrived at an election-night party, wrote the BBC's Gary O'Donoghue. Attendees hugged, kissed and drank to a reality they dared not believe would come true.
Hinojosa becomes the first Latina to be elected governor of the state.
Among the other states where history was made by the Democrats were Kansas, where Adam Hamilton took a closely-fought Senate seat - giving the state its first Democratic senator for nearly a century.
James Talarico, the new US senator in Texas, and Gina Hinojosa, the state's new governor, toast their successes
Among the other firsts of the night were in Florida, where Republican Byron Donalds has become the state's first black governor, following a hearty endorsement from Trump.
Donalds, who will take over the job from Ron DeSantis, said his state was the "envy of the nation", and that he would work to make the state more affordable.
The result was one of the few high points of an otherwise difficult evening for the Republicans.
A win for Bryon Donalds in Florida was one of the few high points for Republicans

In the neighbouring state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, won the governor's race, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.
The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue. Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive.
The state has also not had a Democratic governor for more than 20 years.
Keisha Lance Bottoms beat billionaire businessman Rick Jackson
Elsewhere in the same state, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won a second term in another closely-watched race.

The speculation surrounding Ossoff's plans for the next presidential election in 2028 will likely increase. He is considered a potential leading contender if he throws his hat in the ring, though he has denied having any such plan.
Democrat Jon Ossoff projected to hold key Georgia Senate seat
Democrat Chris Pappas has also made history as the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.

Pappas defeated former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race, whom he thanked on Tuesday, saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."
The 46-year-old Pappas had represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 but chose not to run for re-election so he could launch his campaign for the Senate.

articles.title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night
articles.summary: Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds turned out to be slam-dunks for the Democrats.
body: Watch: The key moments from the US midterm elections
Democrats have torn up Donald Trump's political map on a night that will send shockwaves through American politics for years to come.

With a string of major Senate victories in states that have been reliably Republican for decades - and in Kansas's case, nearly a century - a blue tidal wave crashed across the nation, sweeping Republicans out of power.
Halfway through President Donald Trump's second term, the Democrats now have decisive control of the House of Representatives and have wrested a majority back in the Senate.
They will be able to frustrate Trump's agenda, and launch investigations into his administration. A historic third impeachment attempt could also be on the cards.
Few imagined such an outcome was possible in the months after Trump returned to the White House with unified Republican control of Congress in January 2025.
As the public mood turned against him and his party, Democrats had hopes of retaking the House.
But they contemplated a Senate map that appeared unfriendly, populated by states Trump had won comfortably just two years ago.
Instead, Democrats rewrote the political equations with victories in Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina.

In comments to the BBC's US partner CBS, Trump pledged to strike deals with congressional Democrats, adding that he didn't want to have to spend his final two years in office rejecting their legislation.
He somewhat undermined that sentiment later, posting a picture to Truth Social of his trademark red baseball hat with the word "veto" emblazoned on it.
The president went on to note that his name wasn't on the ballot this year, but if it had been Republicans would have won a decisive victory.
Trump had helped elevate many of those Republican candidates, however, and had urged voters to pretend he was up for re-election.
RESULTS: The latest from around the country
REACTION: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments
GUIDE: What are the US midterms?
In the Senate, Democrats flipped at least six seats, comfortably securing a majority.
Adam Hamilton won in Kansas - a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate almost 100 years ago during the Great Depression.
James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race, ending a 38-year Democratic losing streak in statewide elections there.

In South Carolina, Annie Andrews beat Darline Graham, who had been appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham. Few analysts had that seat in play even a few months ago.
Five-term Republican Susan Collins conceded Maine's Senate election to Democrat Troy Jackson.

Paralympian Josh Turek flipped the Iowa Senate seat held by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Democrats also wrested from Republicans a Senate seat in Ohio, with Sherrod Brown's comeback victory over Jon Husted.
Meanwhile, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has beaten Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's bitterly fought Senate race.
Nor was that the end of the electoral carnage for Republicans.
Ruby-red Texas witnessed another seismic result in the governor's race.
Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, who was earlier this year seen as the prohibitive favourite.
Democrats also took governors' races in Iowa, Ohio and Georgia, which made history by electing the first black woman to such a post.
Meanwhile, the party has won a House majority for the first time since 2022.
They are projected to win 245 House seats and the Republicans 166 seats.
Democrats celebrate in Maine where the party won a crucial Senate race
A look at the key races offers plenty of reasons why.
Democrats flipped House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Kentucky and Colorado, among others. And they were poised to make gains in Virginia and Indiana.

Black Democrats in the southern states turned out in record number, helping to carry their party to victory. And Hispanic voters, whose support had helped secure Trump's presidential victory in 2024, swung decisively back to the Democrats.
Democrats won all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border.
And Hispanic voters helped Democrats hold House seats in Florida that the state's Republicans had sought to flip by redrawing the congressional district lines.
In fact, the congressional redistricting battles that had dominated headlines for months last year ended up being a bust for the Republicans.
In Texas, they had hoped their line-drawing would net five new seats for their party. But on Tuesday they may end up losing one seat.
If there is a silver lining for conservatives, Florida as a whole still appears to tilt to the right.
Republican Senator Ashley Moody narrowly won re-election, as did congressman Byron Donalds, who was elected the Sunshine State's first black governor.
And embattled Republicans were able to hold governorships in Vermont and New Hampshire. But the bright spots were few and far between.
Just two years ago, Trump won the presidency with 48% of the vote. He claimed an electoral mandate.
He then went about governing like it, pushing sometimes unpopular policies on trade and immigration, and launching an Iran war that is opposed by most of the American public.
On Tuesday, voters gave him the kind of stinging rebuke that will not be easily forgotten.

articles.title: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'
articles.summary: The media personality and businesswoman says she's worked on her acting for series two of All's Fair.
body: 'I'm not a quitter': Kim Kardashian on retaking the bar exam

It was meant to be Kim Kardashian's triumphant debut as a leading actor - but last year's legal drama All's Fair was so universally panned by critics that it actually broke streaming records as audiences clambered to see what all the fuss was about.
Kardashian, who is best known as a media personality and businesswoman, tells the BBC she had no choice but to "lean into" the discourse and come back for a second series.
"We thought we were this law show, dealing with some really serious issues," she jokes.
But viewers mostly enjoyed its comedy value - with outlandish outfits and zingy one-liners from co-stars Sarah Paulson and Glenn Close sending the show straight into the pantheon of 'camp classics'.
Kim Kardashian has returned to her role as Allura Grant in Ryan Murphy's legal drama All's Fair

"We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."

All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.
Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian bearing the brunt of criticism.
The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".

But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand.
Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?
"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"
Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down.
"I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.
Kardashian's co-stars Sarah Paulson and Naomi Watts have also returned for season two

While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life, after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.
Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification.
"If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."
But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice, external, she does say she will change how public she is about her studies.

"I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton.
"I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me.
"I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.
All's Fair was criticised in its first series for bad acting, but Kardashian's co-stars say she has stepped up in the next iteration of the show
Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.

Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.
As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season".
"She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."

One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know".
"It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

articles.summary: An impasse between the US and Russia at the UN means its peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has ended after 35 years.
body: Morocco claims Western Sahara as part of its territory

Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.

The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.

The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.
Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.

Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.

Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Algeria became Polisario main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.
The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.

Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.
After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.
The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.
The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.
In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.
Thousands of Moroccans marched into Western Sahara in 1975 in what became known as the Green March
The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.
Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.
The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.

But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.
The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.
It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.
The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.
Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.

Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.
The UN mission has been in Western Sahara since 1991
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.

The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.
Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.
Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.

"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
Thousands of Sahrawis live in refugee camps in Algeria
Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.
Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.
"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.
Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.
He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.

In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: What the Democrat midterms victory tells us about Trump’s future as president
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: A thumping night for the Democrats has seen the party take control of Congress, altering the course of Trump’s second presidency
body: Good morning. While you were sleeping, a political earthquake hit the United States and it’s still climbing up the Richter scale. Voting in Alaska and Hawaii wrapped up only hours ago, but early midterm results streaming in from across the US are making history for the Democrats, as they cash in on Trump’s plummeting popularity.

Democrats have taken control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, and the scale of their successes are far larger, and the speed at which they’ve materialised far quicker, than had been expected. Some of the most hotly contested races of the night have already been called, with Democrats flipping seats in Texas, Ohio and Kansas.

Donald Trump has, with characteristic grace, already blamed the results on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot, saying if he was “we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”. That’s despite the fact he spent the campaign telling voters to pretend it was his name on their paperwork. Later, he appeared on a social media post wearing a hat emblazoned with the word “VETO”.

Today’s First Edition has all you need to know this morning: the latest results, a guide to what comes next, and insights from our senior politics reporter for Guardian US, Chris Stein, in Washington. That’s after this morning’s other headlines.

EU trade deal | Andy Burnham is preparing to announce billions of pounds of trade deals with the EU covering everything from youth visas to pet passports under his vision of a much closer relationship with the bloc.
UK news | A “well-known individual” has failed in his bid to stop two media organisations from publishing allegations of inappropriate sexual activities, the high court has ruled.
UK politics | Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council has been charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child.

UK news | King Charles has said that deepening his understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to address the wrongs of the past, as Caribbean leaders and campaigners intensified demands for an apology and reparations from Britain.

Climate crisis | Countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.

The results you’re waking up to mark a major turnaround for Republican rule. Since the start of Trump’s second presidential term, the party has controlled both chambers of Congress, the US legislative body. This, along with the conservative majority in the supreme court, has given the right free rein over all three branches of the US federal government. Just two years ago, the Democrats looked to be a party with no clear route back to power in Washington DC. Now, a swell of victories has seen them take control of Congress.

Some Democrat gains would have been par for the course: in 90% of midterm elections in the past 80 years, the president’s party has lost House seats. But these wins are massive. In the last couple of hours, results have come in thick and fast – with historic Senate wins for the Democrats in Texas, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and South Carolina – where Democrat Annie Andrews made a shock win in a seat where a Democrat hasn’t been elected to the Senate since 1998. That means the party now has (at least) 53 seats, a clear majority in the 100-member house, and more victories expected.

It’s been a big night of firsts too – in Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan has become the first Native American US senator, in Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley won the gubernatorial race, making history as the state’s first Black governor, and in Kansas, Adam Hamilton has become the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in the state in nearly a century. The House is poised to have its first ever Black speaker in Hakeem Jeffries, who has declared that “America is back”. He said: “Today begins the great American comeback. The American people have spoken all across the land.”
Results from states on US Eastern Time have been making headlines already.

In Georgia, Democrat senator Jon Ossoff, who has been cited as a potential presidential contender in 2028, fought off a challenge from Mike Collins, a Trump-backed congressman. Ohio saw Democrat Sherrod Brown, who represented the state for 18 years before losing in 2024, returning to the US Senate.

If that’s not enough drama, turn your focus to Maine. Republican senator Susan Collins has been in office since 1997, despite the state itself often turning blue in presidential races. An hour ago, she lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson. In Mississippi, the US Senate race is on a knife’s edge with 97% of votes counted – it’s a seat that even the most optimistic of Democrats didn’t predict could be in reach.

Michigan, a swing state that has been one of this election cycle’s mostly fiercely contested, is also looking likely to be taken by the Democrats, according to projections. The senate seat here was already in Democratic control, though the state (narrowly) backed Trump in 2024. There are two key races here with Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official firmly on the left of the Democratic party, hoping to win a Senate seat. If successful, he’ll have fought off not just his Republican rival, former congressman Mike Rogers, but efforts by his former Democratic primary opponent, Haley Stevens, to secure a Republican victory.

And there’s Michigan’s 7th congressional district, where progressive candidate and co-founder of climate activist organisation the Sunrise Movement, William Lawrence, is taking on a Republican incumbent in a seat that oscillates red and blue by the finest of margins. “If they win, the left will argue that progressives and policies like Medicare for All can win in swing territory,” says Chris. “If they fail, centrists will blame left-wingers and the Democratic Socialists of America for hurting the party.”

In Texas Democratic state representative James Talarico executed an impressive campaign, and has beaten sleaze-and-scandal laden Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton – giving a clear signal of American inclinations. “Every billionaire mega donor, every trillionaire mega donor … power belongs to the people,” Talarico declared on his victory.

Texas also has 38 seats in the House of Representatives being contested, and the state has been a focal point for gerrymandering in recent years, with district boundaries redrawn to benefit Republicans. It was previously predicted these changes could hand the Republicans five extra seats but these gains looked not to have materialised. “It’s another sign Latino voters who broke Republican in 2024 won’t do so again,” says Chris.

It took 22 days for Iowa to announce its final results in 2024, but we have its results far sooner this time. The midwestern state hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, but a Dem running on centrist platforms has won here, along with the governorship and three House districts. Much like success in Michigan will be a progressive talking point, victories here will be central to the moderate Democrat narrative.

The west coast is solid ground for the Democrats. Nevada in particular saw Democrats target House seats they viewed as ripe for flipping. In California, redrawn district boundaries (a tit-for-tat response to Texas gerrymandering) will probably see Democrats pick up extra seats.

But really, it’s the Alaska Senate race where your attention should be focused later. Both seats are Republican, something Democratic candidate and seasoned politico Mary Peltola hopes to put an end to. Her chances looked good, entering the race hoping to capitalise on Alaskans anti-Trump sentiments. In the final stretch, however, she has faced allegations of mistreating staff and ballot stacking. And if this one’s close, we’ll be waiting a while: Alaska accepts ballots up to 15 days after the polling day.

All eyes are on the size of the majorities Democrats can now clock up. The Republican majority in the House is wafer thin, so it was widely expected to flip blue. “A good night for Democrats would have been a House majority in the double digits,” says Chris, alongside any size of Senate majority. It’s looking increasingly like both will come to pass.

The consequences could prove pivotal. Control of the Senate will now allow Democrats to reject Trump’s nominees for cabinet positions, ambassador posts and judicial appointments, including to the supreme court, just as two of its conservative justices are thought to be gearing up for retirement. Taking the House, meanwhile, will stymie the Republican agenda, ensuring legislation can only pass through the chamber with Democratic support. Dems will now also have the power to launch investigations into the Trump administration and to impeach federal officials. Hakeem Jeffries has already promised to “hold the crooks accountable”.

With their wins stacking up, there’ll be spin aplenty from both left and right within the Democratic party looking to shape the narrative, as its identity crisis continues. Yesterday’s vote was by all accounts a stonking success, but what next for the party is far from certain. “Their electoral coalition had fallen apart since the Obama years,” says Chris. The party has no clear leader, and remains unpopular, with low favourability ratings. An ideological skirmish will continue into next year’s Presidential primaries.

But, Chris adds, “this resounding victory shows how weak the Republicans are. For the Democrats, these wins are beyond their wildest dreams. Yes, they still have to find a leader, and yes, they have their unpopularity to deal with. Yes, they’ll have to deliver on their governing promises and it’s going to be a messy two years with Trump in the White House still.” But, “this is proof Dems can still win even in the reddest places.”

For Republicans, meanwhile, as the president enters lame-duck territory, the question of what the party looks like post-Trump will need to be answered. “This midterm was fundamentally a test of whether Americans are still behind Trump,” says Chris. By all accounts, they aren’t. “These results take the lustre off of his presidency. It’s a terrible night for him and the Republicans.” And that’s a reality no amount of Truth Social posting can hide.
I’ve not been to Kent before, but I love a hike and a pub trip to follow. Definitely now tempted to try the Darent Valley Path from Shoreham to Eynsford walk. Lysia Wright, newsletters team

Rugby union | Prem Rugby clubs’ collective losses and debt levels are continuing to increase despite growing interest from global companies and financiers.
Football | The Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel has died following a collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during a match in Spain’s second division.
“PM to reveal EU youth visa pact and trade deals worth billions”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The Times splashes “Slavery was evil but we helped end it, says King”, the Mail writes “Britain has leading role in ending the slave trade, says Charles”, and the i Paper has “King says slavery was ‘monstrous’ – but stops short of offering apology”. The Express’s take is “Andy’s plan to say sorry for slave trade will cost us”.

Elsewhere, the Telegraph leads on “Calls to scrap ‘chilling’ trans law”, the FT says “Nvidia demands cut in clients’ China dealing to protect American AI lead”, the Sun splashes “‘Sex pest’ loses gag big” and the Mirror writes “Sex claim star loses bid to hide name”. Lastly Metro, on the fridge cyber-attack, says “Even our spooks are spooked”.
Why are fridges being hacked and what could be next?

Supermarket fridges and freezers in several European countries have malfunctioned after a reported cyber-attack, with their thermostats remotely cranked up. It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack but the EU has condemned what it said was ‘a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply’. It comes as the UK’s cybersecurity body warns AI-powered malicious software is ‘highly likely’ to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028. Lucy Hough speaks to global tech reporter Aisha Down.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

After years of being terrified to move, one bike ride changed Patty Azzarello’s life. When Azzarello was 10 years old she was diagnosed with scoliosis, severe lordosis, where the spine is excessively curved, and spondylolisthesis, meaning a vertebrae was out of place.
She was told that a simple bump or fall could sever her spinal cord, leaving her paralysed. This led to years of anxiety about exercising.

When she moved to Colorado in her 30s, a co-worker invited Azzarello on a bike ride and she accepted, not realising it was a 20 mile ride. Azzarello realised that her body was stronger than she thought. Since then, she’s hiked the Alps and cycled for entire days. Today, at 60, Azzarello remains incredibly active. “I am no longer ashamed of my body,” she says. “It has become my ally.”
